# A.1 Command-line options

Every option JNEXT accepts is listed below, grouped the way the manual groups
them. This page, the **jnext(1)** man page and
[`USAGE.md`](https://github.com/jorgegv/jnext/blob/main/USAGE.md) are three
renderings of one source, so they cannot disagree with each other.

A bare filename is shorthand for `--load`, so `jnext game.tap` works. Anything
starting with `-` is treated as an option, never as a filename, and naming the
program both ways at once is rejected.

For a quick reminder without leaving the shell:

```console
$ jnext --help
$ jnext --version
$ man jnext
```

If you ever find the documentation and the program disagreeing, the program is
right — please [report it](https://github.com/jorgegv/jnext/issues).

A numeric value is taken whole. Trailing characters (`5x`), a value
outside the option’s range, or a negative count are a usage error:
**jnext** prints a message naming the option and the value, and exits
with status 1.

## Machine and program

**--machine** *TYPE*
:   Machine type: `48k`, `128k`, `plus3`, `pentagon`, `next` (default).
    A snapshot given to **--load** (`.jns`, `.sna`, `.szx`, `.z80`) runs
    on the machine it was saved on instead, and **jnext** warns when
    that is not the one given here.

**--load** *FILE*

:   Load a program. The format is detected from the extension: `.nex`,
    `.jns`, `.sna`, `.szx`, `.z80`, `.tap`, `.tzx`, `.wav`, `.rzx`.
    (`.rzx` is accepted here and plays back, as **--rzx-play**.) A
    `.zip` archive holding one of them loads that program, and a NEX in
    one also gets its directory in the archive (see the [`.zip`
    entry](../05-running-programs/index.md#programs-in-zip-archives)).

    `.jns` is jnext’s own whole-machine snapshot (see [5.9
    Snapshots](../05-running-programs/09-snapshots.md)). Loading one
    restores the machine it was taken on, including the machine *type*:
    a `.jns` taken on a Next loads as a Next even if **--machine** says
    otherwise. A `.sna`, `.szx` or `.z80` does the same: it runs on the
    machine it was saved on (the file says which: a `.sna` by its size,
    an `.szx` by its machine ID, a `.z80` by its hardware mode), even
    over **--machine**, which is then warned about. The machine stays
    selected, in the GUI’s **Machine \> Machine Type** too. A snapshot
    from a machine **jnext** does not emulate (a Timex, a Scorpion, a
    Pentagon 512 or 1024), or taken with the TR-DOS, Interface 1, MGT or
    Multiface ROM paged in, is refused, with the reason in the log,
    before anything is changed; at startup **jnext** then exits
    non-zero. A 16K, +2, +2A or +3e snapshot runs as the 48K, 128K, +3
    or +3, and an NTSC 48K `.szx` as a 48K at 60 Hz.

    A NEX file with bytes after the banks its header declares is an
    *extended* NEX. If its header asks for the file to be kept open (any
    non-zero `file_handle`: 1 to 0x3FFF hands the program the handle in
    `BC`, 0x4000 and above writes it at that address), the program can
    read the extra bytes from its own file. If the header says
    `file_handle` 0, jnext does what the Next’s own loader does: it
    loads only the declared banks, ignores the trailing bytes and starts
    the program. More than 16 KB of ignored bytes also logs a warning.

    The debugger’s source map and symbols attach from beside the
    program: *NAME*`.sld` (or *NAME*`.sld.txt`), an sjasmplus source map
    whose labels join the symbols (a label assembled for a page names
    its address only while that page is mapped), beside any program,
    *NAME*`.Memory.txt` (or `Memory.txt`), NextBuild / Boriel ZX Basic
    symbols, beside a `.nex`, and *NAME*`.map`, a z88dk map (`-m`),
    beside a `.nex`, `.tap` or `.sna`: its symbols join the others (not
    when a `Memory.txt` exists; a symbol of a `BANK_n` or `PAGE_n`
    section names its address only while its page is mapped, the others
    take the page mapped at their address when the program is loaded,
    from tape too), and with `-debug` also its source lines, which
    attach when there is no SLD. z88dk’s **-create-app** also writes the
    section binaries (*NAME*`_CODE.bin`, …) that the map is checked
    against; without them it attaches unverified. Beside a tape (`.tap`,
    `.tzx`, `.wav`), whose program is not in memory yet, a map that
    carries a binary identity attaches at once and each memory space it
    covers is checked the first time the program runs its code there; a
    space that does not match drops the map and the symbols that came
    with it, with the reason in the log. A map given with **--map** or
    loaded by hand is kept over them. z88dk’s `--list` listings beside
    the map (*NAME*`.lis`, *FILE*`.lis`) are read too when they match
    the map, and add assembly lines and sdcc’s lines on z88dk 2.4; a
    listing that does not match is skipped with a note in the log. A map
    built for another binary, or a file over 64 MiB, is refused, with
    the reason in the log.

**--nex-args** *LINE*
:   Argument line for a NEX **V1.3** program. *LINE* is placed, verbatim
    and zero-terminated, in the CLI buffer the file’s header declares
    (its address and size). When the program starts, `DE` holds that
    address plus the size - one past the buffer - which is where the
    reference V1.3 loader leaves it (the V1.3 header comment says the
    address itself). A line as long as or longer than that buffer is
    truncated to the buffer’s size with no terminator - which is what
    the reference V1.3 loader does. Quote *LINE* to pass more than one
    word: `jnext --load game.nex --nex-args "level 3"`. Only V1.3
    declares a CLI buffer, so the option is inert - with a warning - for
    a `V1.0`-`V1.2` file, or a V1.3 file whose header declares no
    buffer.

**--experimental-nex-v1.3**
:   Allow loading NEX **V1.3** files. NEX V1.3 is an experimental format
    and is **not supported in any way**; without this flag, loading a
    NEX file whose header version exceeds `V1.2` is refused with an
    error naming the version found (exit status 1). In the GUI,
    selecting such a file shows a warning dialog instead, with Cancel as
    the default. `V1.0`-`V1.2` files are unaffected either way.

**--sdcard** *FILE*
:   Mount SD-card image *FILE* (`.img`). Optional; see [Why JNEXT needs
    an SD-card
    image](../03-first-run/01-why-jnext-needs-an-sd-card-image.md).
    **--sdcard1** is the same option, spelt like **--sdcard2**: each of
    the first card’s options (**--sdcard**, **--sdcard-readonly**,
    **--sdcard-writes**, **--sdcard-writes-reset**,
    **--delayed-sdcard-insert-frames**) also takes the spelling with a
    `1` (**--sdcard1-readonly**, **--sdcard1-writes**,
    **--sdcard1-writes-reset**, **--delayed-sdcard1-insert-frames**),
    and an option together with its other spelling is refused (exit
    status 1). The `1` spellings are not listed by **--help**. A ZIP
    archive is not an image and is refused (exit status 1): unzip it
    first. The WebAssembly build extracts the single `.img` inside one.

**--sdcard-sha256** *HEX*
:   The SHA-256 of the **--sdcard** image, as the caller has already
    checked it. The warm-start recording is keyed on it instead of on
    the image’s size and modification time. **jnext** does not hash the
    image: *HEX* must describe the file as it is. The browser build uses
    this option, because its page rewrites the card into memory on every
    visit (so the time changes) and has already checked the hash. *HEX*
    is 64 hexadecimal digits, in either case. Requires **--sdcard**. A
    recording taken after **jnext** has written to the card in this run
    is used, but not cached.

**--sdcard-download-confirm**
:   Skip the download prompt for the default-location image and proceed.

**--sdcard-download-force**
:   Force re-download and re-patch of the default-location image, to
    recover a corrupted one. Also discards a half-finished download.
    Ignored when **--sdcard** is given: an explicit path always wins.

**--sdcard-upgrade** *MODE*
:   What to do when the default-location card is of an older NextZXOS
    distribution than the one jnext downloads now. *MODE* is **ask**
    (the default in the GUI: forget any “do not ask again” and ask),
    **yes** (upgrade without asking: your files are carried over to the
    new card and the old card is kept as a backup in `previous/`;
    refused when the card has no original image to compare with, and
    then **fresh** is the way), **fresh** (a new card with nothing
    carried over; the old card is kept as the backup), **no** (keep the
    card for this run, no question) or **never** (keep it and do not
    offer this distribution again). Without the option, the GUI asks
    (once, unless “Keep my card (don’t ask again)” was chosen) and
    **--headless** keeps the card and logs one line. Refused together
    with **--sdcard**: an explicit card is never offered an upgrade. See
    [Why JNEXT needs an SD-card
    image](../03-first-run/01-why-jnext-needs-an-sd-card-image.md).

**--sdcard-readonly**
:   Open the SD image read-only, so the host file is never modified. The
    emulated machine sees a write-protected card: writes are rejected
    with the SD write-error token rather than silently discarded. Use it
    when a run must not disturb an image other runs share.

**--sdcard-writes** *FILE*
:   Keep the writes the emulated machine makes to the SD card in *FILE*,
    not in the image: the image is opened read-only and never changes,
    and *FILE*’s sectors are laid over it whenever the card is mounted,
    so the writes survive the next run. *FILE* belongs to one image,
    identified by its **--sdcard-sha256** digest or else by its size and
    modification time: a *FILE* made against another image is refused
    (exit status 1), and so is a file that is not a **jnext** SD-writes
    file. It is created at the first write and holds only the sectors
    the machine wrote (516 bytes each) and the one file jnext’s esxDOS
    stand-in keeps for a directly loaded NEX (see **esxDOS calls from a
    directly loaded NEX**), stored when the program closes it and handed
    back to the stand-in at the next start, whatever the program: it
    belongs to the card, not to the NEX that wrote it. Excludes
    **--sdcard-readonly**; with **--sdcard-file-add** the copy goes into
    *FILE* and the image is not written. Do not change the image with
    another program while *FILE* has writes for it (hdfmonkey, mtools, a
    loop mount, a copy over it): *FILE* would no longer fit the image,
    and the card the machine sees would be damaged. Use the SD card file
    manager (File menu), which writes into *FILE*. JNEXT warns once,
    with a message box and in its log, when the image of a card with a
    writes file changes (or is replaced, deleted or resized) while it
    runs, and it refuses *FILE* at the next start (“was made for another
    image, or the image was changed by another program since”). The same
    applies to **--sdcard2-writes**. A recording of the warm start is
    keyed on the image and on *FILE*’s sectors, so it is taken again
    after the machine has written one; the stand-in’s file is not card
    state and does not change it. Files read from the image by the host
    (the ROMs, a snapshot’s card identity) do not see the writes. See
    [Why JNEXT needs an SD-card
    image](../03-first-run/01-why-jnext-needs-an-sd-card-image.md).

**--sdcard-writes-reset**
:   Discard the writes kept in the **--sdcard-writes** *FILE* before the
    card is mounted, the stand-in’s file included, so the run starts on
    the image as it is. Requires **--sdcard-writes**. A file that is not
    a **jnext** SD-writes file is refused, never removed.

**--no-sdcard**
:   Run a directly loaded NEX with no SD card at all: no NextZXOS, no
    ROMs and no warm start. An emulator convenience, like the esxDOS
    stand-in: a real Next always has its ROMs. The NEX starts on the
    synthetic machine **--load** has always assembled when there is no
    firmware, and every esxDOS call it makes is answered by the
    stand-in: it implies **--esxdos-stub**, so the NEX’s own directory
    is served, unless **--esxdos-stub-root** names another. For a
    program that uses no ROM routine and no NextZXOS service beyond the
    esxDOS file calls. **The ROM area is empty**: the first time the
    program executes code from a ROM (an IM 1 interrupt at \$0038, **RST
    \$10**, a call into the ROM) **jnext** logs an error naming the
    address and the likely cause,
    e.g. `executed ROM code at $0038 (IM 1); --no-sdcard has no ROM`,
    and the program will hang or show garbage. DivMMC and the Multiface
    are held off, the NMI buttons are refused, File \> Insert SD Card
    Image…, Eject SD Card and their second-card twins are disabled and
    the status bar shows **SD: none**. A hard reset runs the boot ROM,
    which stops at its no-card screen as on hardware; the program is not
    loaded again. Requires **--load** of a **.nex** (directly or in a
    **.zip**) on the Next (a machine saved in Preferences other than the
    Next is refused too: give **--machine next**), and excludes every
    **--sdcard** and **--sdcard2** option, **--warm-start-regenerate**,
    **--delayed-sdcard-insert-frames**,
    **--delayed-sdcard2-insert-frames** and **--delayed-nmi**. In a
    browser page it is `card: { source: 'none' }`.

**--sdcard2** *FILE*
:   Mount SD-card image *FILE* (`.img`) in the **second SD card slot**,
    which NextZXOS sees as the next drive after the first card’s
    partitions (D: for a first card with one). There is no default and
    no download: the slot is empty unless this is given. ROMs are read
    from the first card only. A *FILE* that is not a readable regular
    file, a ZIP archive, or the same file as **--sdcard**, is refused
    (exit status 1). It also names the card the SD card commands
    (**--sdcard-file-add**, **--sdcard-file-extract**,
    **--sdcard-writes-flatten**, **--sdcard-export-changes**,
    **--sdcard-import-changes**) act on. See **A SECOND SD CARD**.

**--sdcard2-readonly**
:   Open the second card’s image read-only, as **--sdcard-readonly**
    does for the first. Requires **--sdcard2**.

**--sdcard2-writes** *FILE*
:   Keep the writes the emulated machine makes to the second card in
    *FILE* instead of its image, as **--sdcard-writes** does for the
    first card; *FILE* belongs to that image, identified by its size and
    modification time. Requires **--sdcard2**; excludes
    **--sdcard2-readonly**.

**--sdcard2-writes-reset**
:   Discard the writes kept in the **--sdcard2-writes** *FILE* before
    the card is mounted. Requires **--sdcard2-writes**.

**--sdcard-file-add** *FILE*
:   Copy host *FILE* — a file, or a directory with everything in it —
    into the SD-card image and **exit without starting emulation**.
    Without **--sdcard-file-dest** it lands in the root of the card
    under its own name. Give it once per run. The image written is the
    one **--sdcard** names, or the default-location image when
    **--sdcard** is omitted (your own card); **--sdcard2** *FILE* names
    the second card instead, never both. With **--sdcard-writes**
    (**--sdcard2-writes** for the second card) the copy goes into that
    file instead and the image is not written. When another jnext holds
    the card, the file is copied through that jnext, which must serve
    ZRCP (**--zrcp-port**). See **PUTTING A FILE ON THE CARD**.

**--sdcard-file-dest** *PATH*
:   Optional. The path on the card that **--sdcard-file-add**’s *FILE*
    becomes, from the root of the card (`/NEXTZXOS/DRV-A.DSK`). The
    leading `/` is optional, directories are separated with `/`, and any
    missing directory in the path is created. For a directory, `/`
    copies its contents straight into the root of the card.

**--sdcard-file-force**
:   Let **--sdcard-file-add** replace files that are already there.
    Without it an existing destination file is refused and nothing is
    written.

**--sdcard-file-extract** *PATH*
:   Copy the file, or the directory with everything in it, at *PATH* on
    the SD card (`/GAMES/game.nex`; long or 8.3 names, any letter case)
    into the **current directory** under its own name, and **exit
    without starting emulation**. A local file or directory of that name
    is refused and left as it is. Give it once per run. It reads the
    card **--sdcard** names, or the default-location image when
    **--sdcard** is omitted, as a run with the same options would see it
    (with **--sdcard-writes**, through that file). The image is never
    written; the writes file keeps its contents (as for any run given
    it, it may be compacted). With **--sdcard2** it reads the second
    card (and **--sdcard2-writes**), never both cards. See **GETTING
    YOUR FILES OUT**.

**--sdcard-writes-flatten** *OUT*
:   Write *OUT*, a plain image of the card with the **--sdcard-writes**
    *FILE* laid over it (the card as the machine sees it), and **exit
    without starting emulation**. Any FAT tool (mtools, a loop mount,
    7-Zip) can open *OUT*. Requires **--sdcard-writes**
    (**--sdcard2-writes** for the second card, named with
    **--sdcard2**). An *OUT* that already exists is refused. See
    **GETTING YOUR FILES OUT**.

**--sdcard-go-back**
:   Go back to the previous SD card that an upgrade kept in `previous/`
    next to the default card, and **exit without starting emulation**.
    It is a swap: the card that was in use becomes the backup, your
    **--sdcard-writes** files go with their cards, and the distribution
    you left is not offered again. Exits 0 when done; 2 when there is no
    previous card; 3 when it failed and nothing was changed; 4 when the
    card is in use by another jnext. Refused together with **--sdcard**,
    another SD card command, **--load** or **--inject**.

**--sdcard-delete-backup**
:   Delete the previous SD card an upgrade kept in `previous/`, giving
    its disk space back, and **exit without starting emulation**.
    Nothing else is touched. It exits with the statuses of
    **--sdcard-go-back**, and is refused in the same cases.

**--sdcard-export-changes** *DIR*
:   Copy the files you added or changed on the card, as the machine sees
    it (the card plus the **--sdcard-writes** file, when one is given),
    into *DIR* as ordinary files, write the list `CHANGES.txt` beside
    them, and **exit without starting emulation**. *DIR* must be new or
    empty. What it compares the card against, in this order: the card as
    jnext made it (the default card, when its original image is still on
    disk and matches), the image named by **--sdcard-export-base**, the
    card itself when there is a **--sdcard-writes** file (so only that
    file’s changes are exported); with none of these it refuses. It acts
    on one card: **--sdcard2** names the second one. See **GETTING YOUR
    FILES OUT**.

**--sdcard-export-base** *FILE*
:   With **--sdcard-export-changes**: the image the card was made from,
    to compare against. A raw distribution image is accepted as it is.

**--sdcard-import-changes** *DIR*
:   Put the files of a **--sdcard-export-changes** directory *DIR* onto
    the card (or, with **--sdcard-writes**, into that file) and **exit
    without starting emulation**. *DIR* must hold the `CHANGES.txt` the
    export wrote. A file already on the card is replaced, a read-only
    one too; nothing is ever deleted; the attributes (read-only, hidden,
    system) are restored. All or nothing, as **--sdcard-file-add**. It
    acts on one card: **--sdcard2** names the second one. See **GETTING
    YOUR FILES OUT**.

**--warm-start-regenerate**

:   Discard the cached warm-start recording and take a fresh one on the
    next **--load** of a `.nex` file.

    A **--load** of a `.nex` on the ZX Spectrum Next runs the program on
    a RECORDING of a real firmware boot, not on the machine **jnext**
    assembles. This is the behaviour, not an option: on the first load
    with a given SD image **jnext** cold-boots it (`nextboot.rom` -\>
    `TBBLUE.FW` -\> NextZXOS, a few seconds) and drives NextZXOS to its
    Command Line, where it is executing a typed statement, as it is when
    `.nexload` starts a program; it stores the resulting machine state
    under `~/.jnext/warm-start/`, and applies the program on top of it —
    which is what `.nexload` does on real hardware. Later loads restore
    that state instead of booting. If no recording can be made or used —
    no SD image, a card with no firmware on it, a recording that will
    not load back — **jnext** says so on standard error and falls back
    to the machine it has always assembled.

    The recording is keyed by the SD image’s size and modification time
    (or by the **--sdcard-sha256** digest), the machine type, the state
    format and the recording procedure, and it is also dropped when
    **jnext** itself writes to the image, so it invalidates itself
    whenever any of those change. The image’s contents are not read: an
    image replaced or edited from outside with the same size and the
    same modification time (`cp -p`, `touch -r`) is served the old
    recording. Use this option to force the issue in that case, and
    after replacing `TBBLUE.FW` or NextZXOS on the card. It applies to
    `.nex` files on the Next only: the other machine types run no
    firmware, and snapshots and tapes are loaded by mechanisms a
    firmware-resident machine does not have.

    The recording is made on your machine from the image you mounted,
    and is never shipped with **jnext**: it contains NextZXOS and DivMMC
    ROM content.

**--set** *SECTION.KEY=VALUE*

:   Set one setting of `~/.jnext/jnext.conf` for this run. Every
    Preferences setting can be given this way: the key is the file’s
    `[section]` and key name joined with a dot, the value is what the
    file holds, and the keys are listed under **Settings for --set**
    below. Repeat it for more
    (`--set audio.gain_db=-6 --set startup.silent=false`). The split is
    at the first `=`, so a value may contain one.

    A value that is not accepted, or a key that does not exist, is a
    usage error naming both, and **jnext** exits with status 1. A key
    the running frontend has no use for (a window setting under
    **--headless**, say) is reported with a warning and ignored, so one
    command line can serve all three frontends.

    **Precedence.** The command line wins over the saved `jnext.conf`,
    which wins over the built-in default; a flag and **--set** are the
    same thing, and the later of two settings of one key wins whichever
    way it is spelled (`--cpu-speed 28 --set startup.cpu_speed=0` starts
    at 3.5 MHz). Nothing given on the command line is ever written to
    `jnext.conf`. A change made in the window during the run takes over
    from then on (a **Preferences** OK or Apply, a menu, a file dialog
    that moves the last directory), and **Preferences** shows the saved
    values, not the command line’s.

    A boolean is `true` or `false`. It also reaches what a flag cannot:
    `--set startup.silent=false` plays sound for one run although the
    file says muted, `--set startup.tape_fast_load=true` forces fast
    loading over a saved real-time setting, and
    `--set esp.allowed_hosts=` (empty) allows any host over a saved
    list.

**--cpu-speed** *MHZ*
:   The CPU speed the machine starts at: `3.5`, `7`, `14` or `28`,
    exactly. The same as `--set startup.cpu_speed=0..3`, and like it a
    *starting* value: the speed is programmed through NextREG 0x07 when
    the machine has started, as **Preferences** does. NextZXOS then sets
    its own speed while it boots, as the hardware’s firmware does, so on
    the Next machine a program that waits for the firmware sees the
    firmware’s speed, not this one. On the other machines it holds.
    Works in the Qt window, the SDL-only build and **--headless**.

**--scale** *N*
:   Window scale 1 to 3 for this run, over the saved **Preferences**
    value. The same as `--set startup.window_scale`. Qt window only:
    elsewhere **jnext** warns and ignores it.

**--crt** *EFFECT*
:   CRT effect for this run: `off`, `scanlines`, `soft`, `tv` or `pc`,
    the choices of the **Preferences** CRT effect pop-up. The same as
    setting `startup.crt_filter`, `startup.crt_shader` and
    `startup.crt_shader_style` together. `soft`, `tv` and `pc` need the
    GPU shader; a build without it refuses them (exit status 1) and
    offers `off` and `scanlines`. The Qt window and the browser build:
    elsewhere **jnext** warns and ignores it.

**--speed** *PERCENT*
:   Emulator throttle: 50 = half, 100 = normal, 200 = 2x, 400 = 4x.
    Clamped to 10..1000. Works in the GUI and the SDL-only build;
    **--headless** runs uncapped, so there it has no effect, and
    **jnext** warns.

**--fast-boot** *SECONDS*
:   Run the first SECONDS of a plain Next start at maximum speed with
    the sound off, 0 to 60 (default 15, 0 = off). The firmware splash
    and the NextZXOS start-up pass in a few seconds instead of about
    twelve. It ends at once on the first key the guest sees (Shift is a
    good one: it does nothing else), when the time is up (counted as 50
    frames per second), when a debugger stop happens, or when a load or
    machine change resets the machine; the key is delivered as usual.
    Only the Next machine, and never when a program is loaded at start
    (**--load**, **--inject**, **--rzx-play**), when the command line
    schedules work on the emulated timeline (**--delayed-screenshot**,
    **--delayed-automatic-exit**, **--delayed-pok-frames**,
    **--script**) or when a recording runs. It applies to the launch
    only: a later hard reset boots at normal speed. It never changes the
    emulated machine. To reach the firmware menu, press SPACE while the
    splash shows, or set it to 0.
    `--set startup.fast_boot_hide_screen=true` keeps the window black
    until fast boot ends, so the first picture is the screen it ends on;
    screenshots, recordings and the debugger still see the real screen.
    **--headless** runs uncapped already, so there it has no effect, and
    **jnext** warns. The same as `--set startup.fast_boot_seconds`.

**--when-slow-prefer** *WHAT*

:   What to sacrifice on a host that cannot emulate in real time:
    `audio` (default) or `video`. It changes nothing on a host with
    headroom.

    `audio` keeps the sound card fed by emulating two frames in one
    frame slot when it runs low. The first frame of such a pair is
    overwritten before it can be painted, so the picture advances in an
    uneven, lurching way while the sound stays clean.

    `video` never drops a frame for the sound card. The extra frame runs
    in the next slot instead, so it gets its own present, and the
    machine simply runs slower than real time. The sound queue then runs
    down to its floor and the last sample level is held to bridge the
    gap, which is heard as stutter and a dropped pitch. This is how
    FUSE-style emulators degrade.

    Interactive frontends only; inert under **--headless**, which is
    uncapped and has no audio device. The GUI equivalent is *When the
    host is too slow* under **Settings \> Preferences \> Startup**,
    which applies live.

**--joy1-source** *SRC*
:   Host source for Joy 1 (port 0x1F): `sdl` (autodetected gamepad,
    default), `keys` (host arrow keys, Space = fire) or `none` (nothing
    drives it).

**--joy2-source** *SRC*
:   Host source for Joy 2 (port 0x37): `sdl` (default), `keys` or
    `none`. Only one connector may use `keys`. Interactive (SDL/Qt)
    frontends only; inert under **--headless**.

**--joy1-device** *ID*
:   Physical controller for Joy 1 (port 0x1F), by the id jnext logs when
    it connects it (`Joystick 1 connected: 'name' [id]`): 32 hex digits,
    optionally followed by `#N` to tell identical pads apart. Used while
    the connector’s source is `sdl`; if that controller is not
    connected, jnext logs it and uses the first free one. An empty ID
    chooses Automatic (the first free controller) over a saved
    controller, the same as `--set input.joy1_device=`. Wins over the
    saved choice for this run.

**--joy2-device** *ID*
:   Physical controller for Joy 2 (port 0x37); same form as
    **--joy1-device**, an empty ID included. The two connectors cannot
    name the same controller. Interactive (SDL/Qt) frontends only; inert
    under **--headless**.

**--mouse-release** *METHOD*
:   How a captured mouse is released: `ctrl-alt` (default; Alt+Cmd in
    the Qt GUI on macOS), `middle-click` or `esc`. The methods are
    exclusive: only the one chosen releases. `ctrl-alt` is not consumed
    (Alt still types its compounds); the middle click and Esc are not
    passed to the program. Esc is the ZX BREAK key whenever the mouse is
    not captured, and `middle-click` needs a 3-button mouse. Wins over
    the saved GUI preference for this run. Interactive (SDL/Qt)
    frontends only; inert under **--headless**. The GUI equivalent is
    *Release captured mouse with* under **Settings \> Preferences \>
    Input**, which applies live.

**--touch-keyboard** *MODE*
:   Browser build only: when the on-screen Spectrum keyboard is shown.
    `auto` (default) shows it on a phone or tablet (a device whose main
    pointer is a finger), `on` always, `off` never. A page can also show
    or hide it while it runs (see **The touch keyboard**). Accepted,
    with a warning, and ignored by every other build.

**--joy-uart-rx** *FILE*

:   Attach *FILE* as a serial byte source on the joystick-port UART RX
    pin — the “PC” end of a joy-port serial cable, as used by a dezogif
    / DeZog serial rig.

    The bytes do not reach the guest through either UART header. They
    arrive through the NR 0x0B I/O-mode multiplexer, which the guest
    controls, so the guest hears them ONLY while all three of these
    hold:

    - bits 7 and 5 of NR 0x0B are both set (`joy_iomode_uart_en`),
      i.e. pin 7 is in one of the two UART modes. Modes `00` (static)
      and `01` (CTC-toggled) carry no UART and receive nothing;
    - bit 4 selects the connector this cable is plugged into — see
      **--joy-uart-connector**;
    - bit 0 picks the channel that receives it: 0 = UART 0, 1 = UART 1.
      While the cable owns a channel, the module on that channel’s
      header (the ESP-01 on UART 0, the Pi header on UART 1) can neither
      be heard nor be spoken to, which is what the hardware does.

    Delivery is paced at the receiving channel’s current baud rate, so a
    stream longer than the 512-byte RX FIFO does not overrun a guest
    that is draining it. Bytes sent while the guest is not listening are
    LOST rather than queued, exactly as on the wire — use
    **--joy-uart-rx-delay-frames** to schedule them. If the whole stream
    is lost, jnext says so with a warning rather than finishing quietly.

    An unreadable or empty *FILE* is refused at startup.

**--joy-uart-rx-delay-frames** *N*
:   Hold the **--joy-uart-rx** stream for *N* complete frames before its
    first byte arrives (default 0, i.e. from the first instruction).
    This is how a byte is made to land while the program is already
    running — the asynchronous-break case — rather than being spent
    before the program has set NR 0x0B up. Requires **--joy-uart-rx**.

**--joy-uart-connector** *N*
:   Which joystick socket the joy-port serial cable is in: `1` or `2`
    (default `2`, the connector a real rig uses). NR 0x0B bit 4 selects
    the connector the machine reads, so a guest that selects the other
    one hears nothing at all. Applies to **--joy-uart-rx**,
    **--joy-uart-fifo** and **--joy-uart-pty**, and requires one of
    them.

**--joy-uart-fifo** *PATH*

:   Attach a LIVE, BIDIRECTIONAL serial cable on the joystick-port UART,
    as a pair of FIFOs named from *PATH*: *PATH*`.rx` carries host to
    Next and *PATH*`.tx` carries Next to host. Both names are from the
    guest’s point of view, the same way round as **--joy-uart-rx**.
    Either is created if it does not exist; a path that exists and is
    not a FIFO is refused.

    This is the option to use for a debugger on the host — DeZog driving
    dezogif_ng — because it carries a conversation. **--joy-uart-rx** is
    a RECORDING: it reads its file whole at startup, so pointing it at a
    FIFO waits for the writer to close and then replays what it got. The
    two are mutually exclusive: one cable, one socket.

    The guest side is gated by NR 0x0B exactly as **--joy-uart-rx** is,
    with one asymmetry that is the hardware’s: RECEIVE is
    connector-selected (bit 4 picks one socket’s pin to listen on),
    TRANSMIT is not — the Next presents joystick pin 7 to both sockets
    in turn, so a cable in the socket bit 4 does not select can still
    hear the machine while being unable to be heard by it.

    NOTHING BLOCKS. With no peer attached, received bytes are simply
    absent and transmitted bytes wait; a peer that attaches later gets
    what was queued. A peer that goes away mid-session ends the
    conversation: what was queued is discarded rather than handed to
    whatever connects next, and the cable re-opens for a peer that
    reconnects. Receive is paced at the receiving channel’s current
    baud, so a large host message cannot overrun the 512-byte RX FIFO.

    A rewind or an RZX playback holds the cable INERT — a re-executed
    frame neither re-transmits (the peer cannot un-receive a byte) nor
    consumes host bytes the resumed timeline still needs. Nothing about
    a live cable is saved in a snapshot. Rewinding does not rewind the
    program on the other end of the cable, so a debugger session will
    not survive one.

    POSIX only. Refused in the browser build, which has no named pipes.

**--joy-uart-pty**
:   As **--joy-uart-fifo**, but allocate a pseudo-terminal instead and
    log the slave device path at startup. This is the form a serial
    client opens — DeZog’s serial remote wants one serial device, not a
    pair of pipes — and it is put in raw mode so a binary protocol
    passes through untranslated. POSIX only. Refused in the browser
    build, which has no terminals.

**--nextpi**

:   Start **NextPi** — the software that runs on the Raspberry Pi of the
    Spectrum Next, on its GPIO header — under QEMU (`qemu-system-arm`,
    machine `raspi0`), connected to UART 1, the UART wired to that
    header. NextZXOS’s own Pi tools (`.pisend`, the NextPi UI) then talk
    to a real NextPi. jnext does not emulate the Pi: QEMU must be
    installed, and jnext starts it, wires it in and stops it when it
    exits.

    jnext first checks that QEMU (and, until the first start has made
    the Pi’s overlay, `qemu-img`) is installed, and stops with the
    install hint if not, before anything is offered or downloaded.

    The first run that needs it offers to download NextPi from its
    mirror (<https://zx.xalior.com/NextPi2/>) into `~/.jnext/nextpi` —
    about 6 GB, with about 22 GB free needed while it is unpacked — with
    a progress bar, exactly as the SD-card image is provisioned; later
    runs start at once. An archive `NextPi-<release>.tar.gz` already in
    that directory is checked against its `.md5` beside it (fetched only
    if absent) and unpacked without downloading; a directory that cannot
    be used is reported with the missing file, in the question and in
    the log. An interrupted download (Cancel, a dropped connection, or
    30 seconds without data) is kept as `NextPi-<release>.tar.gz.part`
    and continues on the next run. NextPi then takes about a minute to
    reach its Supervisor prompt (`SUP>`). The release, the directory,
    the QEMU binary, where the Pi’s sound goes and any extra QEMU
    arguments are set under **Settings \> Preferences \> NextPi** (the
    `[nextpi]` section of `~/.jnext/jnext.conf`) or, for one run, with
    **--nextpi-dir**, **--nextpi-release**, **--nextpi-qemu**,
    **--nextpi-audio** and **--nextpi-qemu-args**, which work in a
    headless session too; their defaults are release `1_93D`,
    `~/.jnext/nextpi`, `qemu-system-arm` on `PATH`, and the Next’s
    mixer.

    On Linux and macOS the Pi’s sound reaches the Next’s mixer over I2S,
    as on the real machine: it is mixed with the beeper, the AY chips
    and the DAC, so **--record** and **--wav-record** include it, and NR
    0xA2 enables and mutes it (NextPi’s tools enable it themselves). It
    is 10-bit, as the hardware’s input is, and arrives about 100 ms
    late. Rewinds and RZX playback hold it silent. With NR 0xA2 bit 0
    set it goes to the EAR input instead (port 0xFE bit 6), as a tape
    signal: how a Next loads a tape the Pi plays to it.

    The guest reaches the Pi only while NR 0xA0 bits 5:4 are `11` — UART
    1 on GPIO 14/15, wired for a Pi — which NextPi’s tools set before
    they talk to it. Until then the Pi’s bytes are lost on the wire and
    the guest’s never reach it, as on the real machine; the first such
    loss is logged once. While NR 0x0B gives UART 1 to the joystick
    connector, the Pi cannot be heard either. Host bytes are paced at
    UART 1’s current baud; a rewind or an RZX playback holds the link
    inert, and nothing about it is saved in a snapshot. A soft or hard
    reset leaves the Pi running. A Pi asked for with this option that
    cannot start (no QEMU, a failed download) is an error; declining the
    download is not — jnext then starts without the Pi. On Linux and
    macOS the link is a pair of FIFOs; on Windows (QEMU for Windows, its
    folder on `PATH` or set in Preferences) it is a loopback TCP socket
    QEMU listens on. **--nextpi** starts the Pi with any machine (the
    header and UART 1 are there in every personality); the saved
    preference starts it only when jnext starts the ZX Next. Changing
    the machine while jnext runs neither starts nor stops it.

**--no-nextpi**
:   Do not start NextPi this run, overriding a saved preference that
    enables it.

**--nextpi-dir** *DIR*
:   The NextPi directory for this run (default `~/.jnext/nextpi`), over
    the value saved under **Settings \> Preferences \> NextPi**. An
    empty value means the default. It is used when NextPi starts, so it
    goes with **--nextpi** (or the saved preference, when it starts
    NextPi); given when NextPi is not enabled for the run, this and the
    four options below are ignored, with a warning naming each.

**--nextpi-release** *NAME*
:   The NextPi release for this run: a release name on the mirror, or
    `latest` for the newest one listed there (default `1_93D`). Over the
    saved value; an empty value means the default.

**--nextpi-qemu** *PROGRAM*
:   The QEMU program for this run (default `qemu-system-arm` on `PATH`;
    with a path, `qemu-img` is expected beside it). Over the saved
    value; an empty value means the default.

**--nextpi-audio** *SPEC*
:   Where the Pi’s sound goes for this run: empty for the Next’s mixer
    (the default), `host`, a QEMU `-audiodev` driver such as `pa` or
    `none`, or `wav:`*FILE*. Over the saved value.

**--nextpi-qemu-args** *“ARGS”*
:   Extra QEMU arguments for this run, added after jnext’s own. The text
    is split into arguments on spaces; `'...'` and `"..."` keep spaces
    in one argument; a backslash is an ordinary character; nothing is
    expanded and no shell is involved. Over the saved `qemu_args`. An
    unterminated quote stops NextPi from starting, with a message (an
    error when **--nextpi** asked for it). For example, a second serial
    port for the Pi, on `ttyS0`:
    `--nextpi-qemu-args "-serial telnet:127.0.0.1:2357,server,nowait"`.

**--tape-realtime**
:   Real-time tape loading, at the speed of an actual tape, instead of
    fast load. It sets the one fast/real-time setting (the GUI’s **Tape
    \> Fast Load** toggle) for this run only, overriding the saved
    preference without changing it; **Tape \> Open Tape File**, **File
    \> Load NEX File**, **--load** of a `.tap` or `.tzx`, and the tape
    restored by a `.jns` all follow that setting. The SDL-only build,
    which has no menu and no saved preference, is controlled by this
    option alone.

**--tape-auto-play**, **--no-tape-auto-play**
:   Turn automatic tape play/stop on (the default) or off for this run,
    overriding the saved GUI preference. While on, the tape deck stops
    in the silent gap between two blocks when no program is reading the
    tape, and resumes when one does, so tapes whose BASIC loader is slow
    between blocks load in real time. It does nothing in fast load mode.
    A `.wav` has no blocks and is never paused. Off, the deck runs
    straight through, as a real one does (a TZX “stop the tape if in 48K
    mode” block now stops only on a 48K machine, as the TZX
    specification says, whatever this setting is).

**--tape-save** *FILE*
:   Save to tape, appending to *FILE*; its extension picks the format. A
    `.tzx` or `.wav` records the machine’s tape output (the MIC jack),
    so a program’s own saver is captured as well as BASIC `SAVE`: a
    `.tzx` holds it as standard (0x10), turbo (0x11) or raw pulse (0x13)
    blocks, a `.wav` as 8-bit mono 44100 Hz audio. Any other name
    (`.tap`) captures only blocks SAVEd through the 48K ROM routine. ROM
    saves are instant in all three: a trap at 0x04C2 (with the 48K ROM
    paged at slot 0) takes the block without running the routine. An
    existing file must be of the same format. Also **Tape \> Start
    Saving…** in the window. Cannot be combined with RZX recording or
    playback: the trap skips the ROM routine, which a recording cannot
    replay.

**--esxdos-stub**

:   Answer a few `RST $08` esxDOS calls for any program, for the whole
    session: the version query, one in-memory file and `run sibling.nex`
    chaining. Every other call goes to the code at `$0008`. For programs
    run without NextZXOS; a directly loaded NEX gets a fuller set
    automatically (see [Programs that need
    NextZXOS](../05-running-programs/index.md#programs-that-need-nextzxos)).
    With NextZXOS booted it answers in front of NextZXOS’s own esxDOS
    for those calls, and NextZXOS’s file commands stop working.

    With a NEX to load (**--load**, or a bare file name) and no
    **--esxdos-stub-root**, the directory the NEX is in is served to it
    as if it had been given as *DIR* (below): read-only unless
    **--esxdos-stub-writable** is also given, and in place of the
    in-memory file. To keep the in-memory file, load the NEX without
    **--esxdos-stub**. A NEX loaded from a `.zip` that holds its data
    files is served its directory in the archive with no flag at all
    (see the [`.zip`
    entry](../05-running-programs/index.md#programs-in-zip-archives)).

**--esxdos-stub-root** *DIR*

:   Serve the host directory *DIR* to the guest through the esxDOS file
    and directory calls, instead of the single in-memory file. Implies
    **--esxdos-stub**. Read-only unless **--esxdos-stub-writable** is
    also given. *DIR* replaces the default of **--esxdos-stub**, the
    directory of the loaded NEX, and the directory of a NEX loaded from
    a `.zip` that holds its data files.

    **Which programs see *DIR*, and which do not.** A NEX loaded with
    **--load** sees it, and so do dot commands: those reach the
    filesystem through `RST $08`, which is what jnext intercepts.
    **NextZXOS does not see it** — not its Browser, not its file
    selector, not BASIC’s `LOAD`, not its loader. NextZXOS carries its
    own SD-card driver and its own FAT code in ROM and reaches the card
    directly, without ever executing an `RST $08`, so there is no point
    at which jnext could answer for it. That boundary is permanent and
    deliberate; it is not a limitation that a later version lifts. **To
    put a file where NextZXOS can see it, copy it into the SD-card
    image.**

    Inside *DIR*, paths behave as FAT paths: `/` and `\` both separate
    components, a leading separator is the root of *DIR* rather than the
    host’s root, lookup ignores case, a component can also be given by
    its 8.3 short name, and the drive letters `*:`, `$:` and `c:` all
    mean *DIR*. A path that would leave *DIR*, and any symbolic link, is
    refused; symbolic links are not listed either. Because `\` is a
    separator, a host file whose name contains one cannot be reached —
    FAT cannot name such a file either. Where two host files differ only
    in case and the guest’s spelling matches neither exactly, the first
    in byte order is taken.

    Directory entries carry the host file’s modification time.
    `M_GETDATE` answers from the emulated clock instead, so it follows
    **--rtc**.

    **Do not combine it with a booted NextZXOS.** It implies
    **--esxdos-stub** and inherits its limitation: the file calls are
    then answered in front of NextZXOS’s own esxDOS, and NextZXOS’s file
    commands stop working — `.ls` reports *No such file or dir*. This
    option is for programs jnext loads itself.

**--esxdos-stub-writable**
:   Allow the guest to create, truncate, write, delete and rename files,
    make and remove directories, and set or clear the read-only bit of
    files under **--esxdos-stub-root**, or in the directory of the
    loaded NEX when no root is given (for a NEX from a `.zip`, in the
    extracted copy, never in the archive): the program can delete any
    file there. Off by default, and deliberately a separate flag: a
    guest write changes a real file on the host immediately, and
    rewinding the emulator cannot undo it. Reads are fully rewindable;
    writes, deletions and renames are not.

**--rtc** *“YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS”*
:   Pin the RTC to a fixed date and time (a frozen clock) instead of
    following the host clock, which makes boot screenshots
    deterministic. The ISO `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS` form is also accepted.

**--silent**
:   Disable all sound output (beeper, the three AY/YM chips, DAC/Covox/
    Specdrum). No audio device is opened and the emulator skips PSG and
    mixer sample synthesis entirely, which can measurably speed up
    CPU-bound runs. Tape loading (EAR input) is unaffected.

**--inject** *FILE*
:   Load a raw binary into RAM.

**--inject-org** *ADDR*
:   Load address for **--inject** (hex, `0x` prefix optional, default
    `8000`). Requires **--inject**.

**--inject-pc** *ADDR*
:   Entry point for **--inject** (hex, `0x` prefix optional, default:
    same as **--inject-org**). Requires **--inject**.

**--inject-delay** *N*
:   Wait *N* frames before injecting (default 0). Use around 100 if the
    binary calls ROM routines that need the system variables set up
    first. Requires **--inject**.

## Networking (ESP-01 WiFi)

**--esp**
:   Enable the emulated ESP-01 WiFi module on UART 0. **Off by
    default** - see [5.6
    Networking](../05-running-programs/06-networking.md) for what
    turning it on gives the running program.

**--no-esp**
:   Force the ESP off for this run, overriding a saved GUI preference
    that enables it. Given both, whichever comes last on the command
    line wins.

**--esp-allow** *HOST*
:   Only let the running program connect to *HOST*. Repeatable: give the
    option once per host. *HOST* is a single name - a comma is
    **rejected** rather than taken as a separator or as part of the
    name, because a name that silently matched nothing would look like a
    restriction that is in force when it is not. Matching is exact and
    case-insensitive, with no wildcards, and an IP address must be
    listed as itself. With no **--esp-allow** at all the program may
    name any host (subject to the always-refused addresses in [5.6
    Networking](../05-running-programs/06-networking.md)). Requires
    **--esp**.

**--esp-listen-address** *ADDR*
:   Bind the running program’s `AT+CIPSERVER` to *ADDR*, default
    `127.0.0.1`. *ADDR* is a numeric IP address, never a name - an
    address resolved through DNS could change under you. The default
    means a program that opens a server is reachable only from this
    machine; widening it (`0.0.0.0`) exposes that program to your
    network, which is why it has to be asked for. Nothing listens until
    the program itself sends `AT+CIPSERVER`. Requires **--esp**.

**--esp-ip-address** *ADDR*
:   Report *ADDR* as the module’s own station address instead of the
    default `192.168.1.50`, so a program that recognises its own address
    can be run against the one it expects. It is what `AT+CIFSR` and
    `AT+CIPSTA?` answer, and nothing more: **nothing binds it, nothing
    routes through it**, and the emulated Next cannot be reached at it -
    that is **--esp-listen-address**, which is a real socket. *ADDR* is
    a numeric IP address, never a name, and `0.0.0.0` is refused because
    that is what the module reports while it has no network. Requires
    **--esp**.

**--esp-ip-address-after** *ADDR*
:   Report *ADDR* instead, once the outage ends. Defaults to the
    pre-outage address, which is what a short outage really does; give
    this when the address should come back **different** - a DHCP lease
    that expired during a long outage, or a router that reassigned. It
    is what makes a program’s stale-address handling testable at all:
    across an outage that returns the *same* address, a program that
    caches its address at start-up and one that re-reads it are
    indistinguishable. Requires **--esp-delayed-associate-frames**, and
    takes the same values as **--esp-ip-address**.

**--esp-delayed-disassociate-frames** *N*
:   Take the emulated module off its WiFi network after *N* emulated
    frames, as if the access point had gone away. From then on
    `AT+CIFSR` reports `+CIFSR:STAIP,"0.0.0.0"` instead of the module’s
    address, which is what a real ESP-01 with no association reports and
    what lets a program detect that its address has gone. Nothing else
    changes: connections already open keep running, new ones still open,
    and no unsolicited `WIFI DISCONNECT` is sent - what a real module
    does to traffic during an outage has not been measured, and jnext
    does not invent it. Requires **--esp**.

**--esp-delayed-associate-frames** *N*
:   Put it back on the network after *N* emulated frames, so `AT+CIFSR`
    reports the module’s address again - the same address as before,
    since a short outage does not normally change it. Requires
    **--esp-delayed-disassociate-frames**, and *N* must be greater than
    its value: an outage that ends before it starts is refused rather
    than run.

## Recording and playback

**--record** *FILE*
:   Record video and audio to an MP4. Requires **ffmpeg**(1) on the
    PATH. If the recording cannot be produced (encoder failure, no
    usable output), **jnext** reports the error and exits non-zero. If
    the recording cannot even be started (no **ffmpeg** on the PATH),
    **jnext** exits non-zero immediately, without running the emulation.

**--wav-record** *FILE*
:   Record the mixed stereo output to a 44.1 kHz, 16-bit PCM WAV. Works
    headless and requires neither an audio device nor ffmpeg.

**--wav-record-stems** *DIR*
:   Record the mix as seven 44.1 kHz, 16-bit stereo WAV files in *DIR*,
    one per source: `ay0.wav`, `ay1.wav`, `ay2.wav` (each AY chip after
    its mode and pan, silent while the chip is not in the mix),
    `dac.wav` (left is A+B, right is C+D), `beeper.wav` (EAR and MIC; a
    playing tape and Pi audio sent to EAR are inside it, as the Next
    mixes them as one term), `pi.wav` (the Pi I2S audio) and `mix.wav`.
    The stems are taken before the host gains and the debugger mutes, so
    `mix.wav` equals **--wav-record** at 0 dB, and the six source files
    add up to `mix.wav` exactly while every source is steady within an
    output sample and otherwise within 3 counts per sample (the rounding
    of the seven files). *DIR* is created if missing and files of those
    names in it are overwritten. If *DIR* or a file cannot be created,
    **jnext** exits non-zero without running the emulation; a write
    error that shows later exits non-zero too. Cannot be combined with
    **--silent**.

**--dac-trace** *FILE*
:   Record `segment,tstate,channel,value` rows for physical DAC writes.
    A cold boot starts a new segment.

**--audio-log** *FILE*
:   Record the decoded audio writes to a CSV, one row per write, with
    the frame, line, hc and T-state it happened at. Rows cover AY
    register writes, the TurboSound chip-select and pan commands (and
    every discarded 0xFFFD write), DAC channel writes (one row per
    channel written), the NextREG 0x2C-0x2E DAC mirror writes and beeper
    EAR/MIC changes, and every write the hardware discarded with its
    reason. Plain AY register selects, border-only writes to port 0xFE
    and the frames a rewind replays are not recorded. The first line is
    the header
    `frame,line,hc,tstate,cycle,pc,source,target,chip,reg,value,prev,flags,reason,port`.
    `frame`, `line`, `hc`, `tstate`, `cycle`, `chip`, `reg` and `flags`
    are decimal; `pc` and `port` are `0x%04X`; `value` and `prev` are
    `0x%02X`. `source` is `cpu`, `dma`, `copper` or `debugger` (writes
    made by the debugger or a script carry `debugger`), `target` is
    `ay`, `ay_select`, `dac`, `dac_mirror` or `beeper`, and `chip` is
    empty for a discarded DAC write that reached no channel. A reset, a
    state load or a rewind adds a row with `marker` in `source` and
    `reset`, `load` or `rewind` in `target`. After a `rewind` row the
    following rows may carry earlier cycles: the file is append-only and
    the rows before the marker are kept. It works in every frontend,
    headless, with **--silent** and in a browser page. An unwritable
    *FILE* is refused before the machine starts. A write error, or
    writes lost because more than 65536 arrived between two services of
    the loop, makes the run exit non-zero.

**--psg-record** *FILE*
:   Record each AY chip’s register stream as `.psg`, in the layout Fuse
    writes for its AY log: a 16-byte header, then for every frame in
    which a register from R0 to R13 was written the register/value pairs
    in register order, with frame separators between the frames. *FILE*
    takes AY#0; AY#1 and AY#2 go to *FILE* with `-ay1` or `-ay2` before
    the extension (`tune.psg` gives `tune-ay1.psg`), created at that
    chip’s first write and aligned to the start of the recording. When a
    register is written more than once in a frame the last value is
    kept. R14 and R15 are not recorded. A reset or a state load keeps
    the elapsed time, and a rewind keeps what was written and carries on
    after it. It works in every frontend, headless, with **--silent**
    and in a browser page. An unwritable *FILE* is refused before the
    machine starts. A write error makes the run exit non-zero. The same
    recording starts from the Chips tab of the debugger’s Audio panel.

**--audio-gain-db** *DB*
:   Set master host audio gain from -24 dB to +24 dB (default 0 dB). The
    gain is applied after the emulated hardware mix; overflow saturates
    at the 16-bit PCM limits.

**--audio-gain-beeper-db** *DB*
:   Set host gain for beeper EAR/MIC/tape-EAR audio from -24 dB to +24
    dB.

**--audio-gain-ay0-db** *DB*
:   Set host gain for TurboSound AY chip 0 from -24 dB to +24 dB.

**--audio-gain-ay1-db** *DB*
:   Set host gain for TurboSound AY chip 1 from -24 dB to +24 dB.

**--audio-gain-ay2-db** *DB*
:   Set host gain for TurboSound AY chip 2 from -24 dB to +24 dB.

**--audio-gain-dac-db** *DB*
:   Set host gain for Specdrum, Soundrive and Covox DAC audio from -24
    dB to +24 dB.

**--rzx-play** *FILE*
:   Play back an RZX recording from the start of the run. Works the same
    in the GUI, the SDL-only build, under **--headless** and in a
    browser page. A recording that fails to load is logged, and
    **jnext** then exits non-zero. The machine starts exactly as it does
    for **--load** *FILE*, so the two spellings replay identically, and
    so do **File \> Load NEX File…** and **File \> Play RZX Recording**
    in the GUI. The recording brings its own snapshot of the machine, so
    it cannot be combined with **--rzx-record**, with **--load** or
    **--inject** of another program, or with a second RZX file. It plays
    on the machine it was recorded on, whatever machine is configured: a
    recording **jnext** makes names its machine, and one from another
    emulator is judged by its embedded snapshot (an SNA’s size, an SZX’s
    machine ID, a `.z80`’s hardware mode). A recording that names none —
    one **jnext** 1.0.0 or earlier made with an SNA snapshot, or one
    whose snapshot is of a machine **jnext** does not emulate — plays on
    the configured machine. An explicit **--machine** given with the
    recording wins, and **jnext** warns when it disagrees with the
    recording, which then goes out of step; a recording played from the
    GUI’s menus always gets its own machine. The recording’s machine
    stays selected afterwards, in the GUI’s **Machine \> Machine Type**
    too, as if chosen there.

**--rzx-record** *FILE*

:   Record input to an RZX file from the start of the run — or, with
    **--load** or **--inject**, from the moment that program is in the
    machine, so the snapshot the file carries is the program, and
    playback replays it. The file is written when **jnext** exits (or,
    in the GUI, at **File \> Stop RZX Recording**). Works the same in
    the GUI, the SDL-only build and under **--headless**. A browser page
    refuses it and records from JavaScript (see THE BROWSER BUILD).
    While recording, a tape loads in real time: a fast load skips the
    ROM loader, which a recording cannot replay. The snapshot is an SZX
    on the 128K, Pentagon and +3 and a 48K SNA on the 48K. The file
    names the machine it was recorded on, which **--rzx-play** then
    uses.

    **Recording is not available on a ZX Spectrum Next, which is jnext’s
    default machine, so this needs an explicit --machine 48k, 128k,
    pentagon or plus3.** An RZX carries a snapshot of the machine it
    starts from plus a log of the values the program read from ports —
    and the log records the values without the ports they came from. So
    no snapshot an RZX can carry both describes a Next (none of SNA, SZX
    or Z80 holds its extra RAM, NextREGs, Layer 2, tilemap, sprites or
    Copper) and keeps the value log aligned with what the restored
    machine goes on to read. jnext refuses rather than write a file that
    looks fine and replays wrong. **--rzx-play** still plays a Next
    recording made by an earlier jnext, with a warning that it may not
    replay faithfully. A *FILE* that cannot be written is refused before
    the machine starts, and a recording that cannot be saved when it is
    written is logged; either way **jnext** exits non-zero. A reset ends
    the recording: a hard reset (the Reset button, F1, or the program’s
    own), loading another program from the GUI, changing the machine
    type, or F4 writes the file there, and nothing after it is recorded
    — a recording cannot replay a reset.

**--rewind-buffer-size** *N*
:   Frame-snapshot ring buffer for backwards execution. Opt-in; default
    0 = off.

**--trace**
:   Enable the per-instruction trace log (a 10K-entry ring). Also
    enabled implicitly by **--rewind-buffer-size** *N* with *N* \> 0,
    and toggleable in the debugger.

**--coverage**
:   Record memory coverage from the start: for every byte of every
    memory (each RAM page, ROM image, DivMMC and Multiface window, Layer
    2 mapping, …) whether the program executed it (first opcode byte of
    an instruction), read it or wrote it. Toggleable in the debugger
    (Debug \> Coverage), where the Disassembly, Memory and Source views
    show it. With the SDL frontend or **--headless** it records but
    there is no viewer; it logs one summary line at exit. Costs a little
    speed while on (3-8% in release builds); no measurable cost while
    off.

## Headless and automation

**--headless**
:   Run with no display and no audio device, at maximum speed.

**--benchmark** *N*
:   Headless only. Run exactly *N* frames uncapped, print one
    machine-parseable `BENCH` line (wall seconds, fps, T-states/s,
    T-states/frame, CPU speed, host core, build type) plus a human
    summary to stdout, then exit. Used by `make bench`
    (`test/bench/bench.sh`).

**--benchmark-label** *NAME*
:   Workload label printed verbatim in the `BENCH` line (default: the
    loaded file’s basename, or `boot-<machine>`). No whitespace, since
    the `BENCH` line is space-delimited. Requires **--benchmark**.

**--delayed-screenshot** *FILE*
:   Save a screenshot after a delay. The format is taken from *FILE*’s
    extension: `.scr` writes the raw ULA screen memory, anything else
    writes a PNG of the composited picture. See **SCREENSHOT FORMATS**
    below. The capture is taken from the next frame the machine renders,
    so if it comes due while the machine is paused - by the debugger, or
    by a **--magic-breakpoint** - it waits until the machine runs again;
    it is never written from the frame that was on screen before the
    pause. One still waiting when the exit comes is an error (see
    **--delayed-automatic-exit**).

**--delayed-screenshot-time** *N*
:   Delay in emulated seconds (default 10; see *Emulated seconds* under
    HEADLESS MODE). Requires **--delayed-screenshot**.

**--delayed-screenshot-frames** *N*
:   Delay in frames. Overrides **--delayed-screenshot-time**. Requires
    **--delayed-screenshot**.

**--delayed-screenshot-layers** *LIST*
:   Layers to compose into the screenshot: a comma-separated list of
    `ula`, `layer2`, `sprites`, `tiles`, `all` (default `all`). Requires
    **--delayed-screenshot**, and is rejected when that screenshot is a
    `.scr`, which has no layers to choose from.

**--delayed-automatic-exit** *N*
:   Exit the emulator after *N* emulated seconds (see *Emulated seconds*
    under HEADLESS MODE). The exit always fires, but work the command
    line deferred to a later frame and that has not happened by then is
    an error, and **jnext** exits non-zero: a **--load** still waiting
    out its boot delay (100 frames for `.tzx` and `.wav`), an
    **--inject** with **--inject-delay**, an **--rzx-record** waiting
    for that load, a **--delayed-keypress**, **--delayed-nmi** or
    **--delayed-screenshot** still to come, a **--joy-uart-rx** stream
    still held by **--joy-uart-rx-delay-frames**, and an edge of the
    **--esp-delayed-disassociate-frames** /
    **--esp-delayed-associate-frames** outage not yet reached. Give the
    exit headroom over the last of them.

**--delayed-automatic-exit-frames** *N*
:   Exit after *N* frames. Overrides **--delayed-automatic-exit**, and
    keeps its rule on work still to come.

**--delayed-snapshot** *FILE*
:   Headless only: requires **--headless**. Save a snapshot after a
    delay in frames. The format is chosen by the extension of *FILE*:
    `.jns`, `.szx`, `.nex`, anything else `.sna`. A snapshot is only
    ever taken at a frame boundary, so if the debugger has paused the
    machine part-way through a frame — a magic breakpoint, say — the
    frame in flight is completed first and the snapshot is written from
    the boundary that follows it. That pause never refuses the capture;
    the saved machine is then up to one frame past the point the
    debugger stopped at. A format that cannot represent the current
    machine *is* refused — it writes nothing, says why, and exits
    non-zero (see [5.9
    Snapshots](../05-running-programs/09-snapshots.md)).

**--delayed-snapshot-frames** *N*
:   Delay in frames for **--delayed-snapshot** (default 0). Requires
    **--delayed-snapshot**.

**--snapshot-compression** *STATE*
:   Whether `.jns` snapshots are written deflated. `on` (the default)
    deflates every member; `off` stores them instead, so the file is
    readable with `unzip -p` and a hex editor at roughly five times the
    size. A debugging aid; it changes nothing about what the file
    contains, and jnext reads both forms. Any other *STATE* is an error.

**--quick-snapshot-keep** *N*\|`unlimited`
:   How many quick snapshots **File \> Quick Save Snapshot** keeps in
    `~/.jnext/snapshots/`: after each save the oldest beyond *N* are
    deleted (default 20; *N* is 1 to 1000000). Only files named exactly
    like Quick Save’s own (`jnext-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.jns`, optional `-NN`)
    are ever deleted; anything else in the folder is left alone.
    `unlimited` keeps everything. Overrides the `[snapshot] quick_keep`
    setting for the run; the SDL-only build, which reads no
    configuration file, takes only this option.

**--snapshot-mode** *MODE*

:   How much a `.jns` load refuses. One setting with three positions,
    because they are one axis and asking for two of them at once is not
    a thing to want.

    `normal` (the default) warns about a mismatched state model revision
    or mismatched ROM digests and refuses a different SD card.

    `strict` turns those provenance warnings into refusals: a snapshot
    written by a jnext whose state model this build does not know, or
    one whose recorded ROM digests differ from the ROMs now loaded. A
    missing tape file is **not** covered — that always warns and never
    refuses, because a machine restores perfectly well without the tape
    it was loading from. The same goes for a tape that has changed or
    whose position cannot be restored.

    `force` restores even though the mounted SD card is not the one the
    snapshot was taken on, printing a warning that names both cards.
    This is the setting that lets you create exactly the silently-wrong
    case the identity check exists to prevent, which is why it is
    spelled out in full.

    Any other *MODE* is an error.

**--delayed-keypress** *SECS* *KEY*
:   Press *KEY* after *SECS* emulated seconds (see *Emulated seconds*
    under HEADLESS MODE). Headless only (requires **--headless**),
    repeatable.

**--delayed-keypress-frames** *N* *KEY*
:   Press *KEY* after *N* emulated frames. This is the frames-unit
    spelling of **--delayed-keypress**, not an override of it: both
    forms queue into the same list, so giving both schedules two
    keypresses. Requires **--headless**.

**--delayed-nmi** *SECS* *BUTTON*
:   Press an NMI *BUTTON* after *SECS* emulated seconds (see *Emulated
    seconds* under HEADLESS MODE). Headless only (requires
    **--headless**), repeatable. *BUTTON* is case-insensitive and names
    which button to press, spelled as the label on a real Next’s case.
    Of its three buttons, two raise an NMI: `nmi` (aliases `mf`, `m1`)
    is the **NMI** button, wired to the Multiface; `drive` (alias
    `divmmc`) is the **DRIVE** button, wired to the DivMMC. **RESET** is
    not an NMI button and is not accepted here. The press goes through
    the same path as the host F9 / F10 hotkeys, so it is subject to the
    same enable gates — NextREG 0x06 bit 3 for the Multiface, bit 4 plus
    NextREG 0x83 bit 0 for the DivMMC — and a press with its gate closed
    does nothing, exactly as on hardware. One press generates one NMI,
    not a repeating one.

**--delayed-nmi-frames** *N* *BUTTON*
:   Press *BUTTON* after *N* emulated frames. This is the frames-unit
    spelling of **--delayed-nmi**, not an override of it: both forms
    queue into the same list, so giving both schedules two presses.
    Requires **--headless**.

**--delayed-sdcard-insert-frames** *N* *FILE*
:   Insert SD-card image *FILE* after *N* emulated frames, exactly as
    **File \> Insert SD Card Image** does (see [Why JNEXT needs an
    SD-card
    image](../03-first-run/01-why-jnext-needs-an-sd-card-image.md)). The
    card keeps **--sdcard-readonly**. The run exits non-zero if the
    insert is refused - while an RZX recording is made or played, while
    a directly loaded NEX keeps its own file open, when *FILE* is not a
    readable file, or when another insert is due in the same frame - or
    if the automatic exit comes first. An empty *FILE* is rejected.
    Repeatable. Requires **--headless**.

**--delayed-sdcard2-insert-frames** *N* *FILE*
:   The same for the **second SD card** slot: insert *FILE* there after
    *N* emulated frames, as **File \> Insert Second SD Card Image** does
    (see **A SECOND SD CARD**). The card keeps **--sdcard2-readonly**.
    The run exits non-zero under the same refusals as
    **--delayed-sdcard-insert-frames**, and when *FILE* is the image the
    first slot has mounted. NextZXOS finds its drives at start-up, so to
    see the card use a hard reset (the environment variable
    `JNEXT_DELAYED_RESET_FRAMES`, or NextZXOS’s own). Repeatable.
    Requires **--headless**.

**--delayed-pok-frames** *N* *FILE*
:   Apply trainers from the POK file *FILE* after *N* emulated frames,
    once the program has loaded. This is how a `.pok` file is used in
    the runs that have no **Machine \> POK Trainers…** window:
    **--headless** and the SDL-only build’s window (see **POK TRAINERS**
    under LOADING PROGRAMS). The trainers are the ones
    **--pok-trainers** names, which this requires. *N* counts frames
    from the start of the run (50 a second on a 50 Hz machine), and a
    tape takes many; the trainers are written through the debugger’s
    memory path, exactly as the window’s **Apply** writes them. Given
    once. The file and the list are checked before the machine starts,
    and a run that fails the check exits 1 without starting: *FILE*
    unreadable, larger than 1 MiB or without a trainer, a listed trainer
    the file does not have or whose lines are malformed, a value missing
    or given where none is open. Later, the run exits non-zero if a
    trainer cannot be applied - an address that is ROM in the current
    memory map, a bank the machine does not have, an RZX recording or
    playback - and then the trainers before it stay applied; and if the
    automatic exit comes first. The Qt window refuses the option; with
    **--headless** every build accepts it.

**--pok-trainers** *LIST*
:   The trainers **--delayed-pok-frames** applies: their numbers in the
    POK file (1 is the first `N` line), comma-separated, no blanks, each
    *T* or *T*`=`*VALUE*. A trainer that leaves a value open (a `256` in
    the file, “Lives” without saying how many) needs *T*`=`*VALUE*,
    *VALUE* 0 to 255, which goes everywhere the trainer leaves one open;
    any other trainer takes none. `1,3=9,7` applies trainers 1, 3
    (with 9) and 7, in that order. A trainer whose bytes memory already
    holds is left as it is. Requires **--delayed-pok-frames**.

**--compositor-trace** *FILE*
:   Dump a per-pixel compositor trace (CSV) for one frame.

**--compositor-trace-frame** *N*
:   Target frame for **--compositor-trace** (default 250). Requires
    **--compositor-trace**.

*KEY* is case-insensitive and is one of: a single character (`a`-`z`,
`0`-`9`, `.`, `,`, `;`, `:`), one of the symbolic names `ENTER`,
`RETURN`, `SPACE`, `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, or a compound
`sym+`*char* / `caps+`*char* (for example `sym+m` is `.`).

## Debugging

**--magic-breakpoint**
:   Enable the magic-breakpoint opcodes (`ED FF`, `FD 00` and `DD 01`).

**--persistent-breakpoints**
:   Keep breakpoints and watchpoints armed while the debugger window is
    **closed**. Without this option — the default — closing the window
    disarms them, and nothing stops. With it, a hit pauses the machine
    and reopens the debugger window at the breakpoint. With the window
    already open, behaviour is unchanged. The breakpoint check then runs
    on every instruction for the whole run, which is what “persistent”
    costs; it is accepted but has no effect in **--headless**, in the
    SDL-only build and in builds without the debugger, since only the
    debugger can set a breakpoint.

**--debugger**

:   Start the program under the debugger: the machine starts **paused**,
    where the program starts, instead of running. The stop is, for a
    **NEX** file, its entry point (a NEX whose entry is 0 is a load-only
    file: the CPU is parked, and that is where it stops); for a snapshot
    (**SNA**, **Z80**, **SZX**, **JNS**) or an **RZX** recording, the PC
    it restores; for **--inject**, the injected program’s PC; with no
    file, power-on, before the first instruction (PC 0). It stops right
    after the program is loaded, before it has run an instruction. A
    tape (**TAP**, **TZX**, **WAV**) stops at the first instruction
    fetched from memory the tape loaded, after its last block has loaded
    (the program it started; in a **TAP** or **TZX**, in fast or
    real-time mode alike); a tape that cannot carry code (BASIC and a
    SCREEN\$ only) stops at the first instruction after its last block.
    A BASIC program that runs code from a REM stops at the end of its
    last block, not in the REM, and a tape that loads code which never
    runs is never stopped (use **--break-at**). A **WAV** has no block
    structure to tell a code tape from a BASIC one, so it always takes
    the code rule: a BASIC-only WAV is never stopped, and a recording
    with noise in its trailing silence can stop late (the end of the
    tape is taken as the last signal edge). A trailing pure-data or
    direct-recording TZX block counts as data in real time only (fast
    load never plays it). The stop is logged
    (`debugger: stopped at $8000 (the NEX entry)`).

    In the Qt GUI the debugger window opens, paused. In **--headless**
    and the SDL-only build there is no window, so the run waits for a
    remote debugger and serves DZRP on port 11000 (DeZog’s `cspect`
    remote) unless a protocol port is given: with **--zrcp-port** or
    **--gdb-port** only those are served, and an explicit
    **--dzrp-port** is used as it is. The same applies to a Qt build
    made without the debugger. A paused headless run waits for the
    debugger without using the CPU, and a debugger that attaches finds
    the machine already paused. Stops in these two frontends pause and
    wait for the remote instead of ending the run with exit code 3:
    under **--script**, a `stop` or a failed `assert` pauses, and a
    script’s own `exit` still exits. Not available in the browser.

**--break-at** *ADDR\|SYMBOL*
:   Implies **--debugger**, and replaces its default stop: run to
    *ADDR*, stop there once, and stay paused. It takes the forms the
    debugger’s Breakpoints panel takes for an Execute breakpoint: a
    hexadecimal address (`8000`, `$8000` or `0x8000`; there is no
    decimal form, so `32768` is not an address), a symbol of the
    program’s own map or of **--map**, `@symbol` (always the symbol,
    even when its name reads as hex), or a source line `file:line` of a
    loaded source map. A symbol or line keeps the memory it was
    assembled for: it stops only while that memory supplies the code.
    The stop is armed when the program is loaded, before it has run, so
    it also catches code a tape runs while it loads. It fires once and
    never appears in the Breakpoints panel. A value that is not an
    address, a symbol or a source line is refused when the program is
    loaded, before it has run an instruction, with exit code 1. Another
    client’s pause before the stop does not cancel it: DeZog attaching
    (which pauses the machine) while a tape loads, then continuing,
    still ends at the stop. Not available in the browser.

**--dzrp-port** *PORT*
:   Serve the DeZog Remote Protocol (DZRP) on TCP *PORT*, so DeZog - or
    any other DZRP client - can debug the running machine; see **REMOTE
    DEBUGGING (DEZOG)**. Off unless given. *PORT* `0` binds a free port
    the system chooses, and the log says which
    (`dzrp: listening on 127.0.0.1:40123`). One client at a time: a
    second connection is closed at once. A port that cannot be bound
    (already in use, say) is a startup error. Works in every frontend,
    **--headless** included.

**--gdb-port** *PORT*
:   Serve the GDB remote serial protocol on TCP *PORT*, so `z88dk-gdb`
    can debug the running machine; see **REMOTE DEBUGGING (Z88DK-GDB)**.
    Off unless given. *PORT* `0` binds a free port the system chooses,
    and the log says which (`gdb: listening on 127.0.0.1:40125`). One
    client at a time. A port that cannot be bound is a startup error.
    May be given together with **--dzrp-port**: each server has its own
    port and its own client. Works in every frontend, **--headless**
    included.

**--zrcp-port** *PORT*
:   Serve the ZEsarUX remote command protocol (ZRCP) on TCP *PORT*, so
    DeZog (its `zrcp` remote) - or `telnet`, or any other ZRCP client -
    can debug the running machine; see **REMOTE DEBUGGING (ZRCP)**. Off
    unless given; `10000` is the port those clients assume. *PORT* `0`
    binds a free port the system chooses, and the log says which
    (`zrcp: listening on 127.0.0.1:40123`). One client at a time: a
    second connection is told so and closed. A port that cannot be bound
    is a startup error. Works in every frontend, **--headless**
    included, and alongside **--dzrp-port** and **--gdb-port**. A second
    jnext’s **--sdcard-file-add** on a card this jnext has open is
    copied through this server (see **PUTTING A FILE ON THE CARD**), so
    the machine that has the card is the one that writes to it.

**--debug-channel** *PROTOCOL*
:   Browser page only: serve the debugger protocol *PROTOCOL* (`dzrp`,
    `zrcp` or `gdb`) to the page’s debug channel, the `debug` option of
    `jnext.mount`. May be given once for each protocol. Every other
    build refuses it with exit status 1, because a server that was asked
    for and cannot be reached is a startup error: use **--dzrp-port**,
    **--zrcp-port** or **--gdb-port** there.

**--debug-listen-address** *ADDR*
:   Bind address for the debugger protocol servers (**--dzrp-port**,
    **--gdb-port**, **--zrcp-port**), default `127.0.0.1`. *ADDR* is a
    numeric IP address, never a name - an address resolved through DNS
    could change under you - and anything else is refused at startup.
    The default means only this machine can reach the debugger; a
    non-loopback address (`0.0.0.0`) exposes it to your network, and
    none of the debugger protocols has any authentication. Refused
    unless a server port is given too: an address for servers that are
    all off would configure nothing.

**--script** *FILE*
:   Load a debugger script (`.jds`); see [Debugger
    scripting](../06-debugger/scripting/index.md). Repeatable: the
    scripts load, and their rules run, in the order given. A script that
    cannot be read, or that has any error, is reported as
    *file*:*line*:*column*: *message* and jnext exits 1 before the
    machine runs - nothing of it runs partially. With **--load**, a
    script that names a source line (`on execute main.c:19`), an
    `@symbol` that **--map** does not know, or a z88dk **--map** symbol
    of a section that names no page waits, with the scripts after it,
    until the program is in (it is still read and parsed at once); an
    error then also exits 1. Its rules start at the load: an `on frame`
    *N* or a **--script-key** due before it never fires (a `.tzx` or
    `.wav` loads about 100 frames in), so give such rules in an earlier
    script that names neither. In **--headless** and the SDL-only build
    a script decides the exit status: `exit` *N* exits *N*, a `stop` or
    a failed `assert` exits 3, a run-time error exits 1. In the Qt GUI a
